**BORR: story and what could move it (as of 8:55 AM CT, 11-25)**

**Setup.** Borr is a leveraged jack-up (shallow-water offshore) driller. Its sinking rig, thin earnings and heavy debt make it a high-beta name.
- Gross borrowings are $2.53B. All 29 rigs are pledged as collateral. Contracted backlog is $928M.
- Q3 (reported 11-18): revenue $263.1M, up 13% from Q2. Adjusted EBITDA $78.9M, up 80% from Q2. Net loss $38.7M, or $0.13 a share, which missed the roughly $0.09 estimate.
- Q2's much larger loss came mostly from a one-time refinancing charge ($176M).
- Guidance: Q4 EBITDA broadly in line with Q3. Full-year 2027 EBITDA broadly in line with 2026. Q1 2027 is expected to dip, then ramp strongly into Q4 2027.
- The stock was about $3.21 to $3.24 in early November, so the recent +22% over five sessions came after earnings.

**Prospector 5 (the main overhang and possible catalyst).**
- The rig sank offshore Gabon on 10-24 during jacking operations. Reports of crew deaths and missing crew conflict, from 1 dead and 4 missing to 3 dead and 2 missing.
- It was declared a total loss. It was insured for $200M, and there is no loss-of-hire coverage.
- WorldOil said the insurance payment was due 11-24. The 247WallSt write-up of the Q3 report said the claim was still awaiting underwriter approval. I found no confirmation that the money has arrived.
- A payout announcement would be an upside catalyst. The packet's disclaimers say the proceeds will go toward use and timing described in the deck, but the excerpt was trimmed, so I couldn't read the stated use.
- A delay or dispute would hurt the stock. A larger-than-expected liability or wreck-removal cost would also hurt.
- Borr also expects to amend its super-senior revolver. That is another near-term balance-sheet item.

**Insider buying.**
- The Form 4 shows Tor Olav Trøim, a director, bought 1,000,000 shares on 11-24 at $3.9373 through Drew Holdings. That is about $3.94M, and the Form 4 shows his indirect holding at about 50.1M shares afterward.
- This is the largest of his 2026 buys, and it is much larger than the September buy of 150,000 shares at $4.38.
- His earlier 2026 buys were at about $4.4 to $5.2, so he is averaging down and has been early before. The Form 4 shows the filing as an open-market buy, code P.

**Market and technicals.**
- Jack-up utilization is about 90%, and Borr's own fleet is near 97 to 99%. Dayrates have recovered from their 2025 lows but are uneven.
- Borr says supply is constrained, with about 30% of the global fleet beyond retirement age.
- Mexico and Pemex receivables are a recurring risk. Two Mexican contracts, for the Odin and Hild rigs, were terminated earlier because of sanctions on the client. Hild has since been redeployed to Nigeria.
- The stock is flat on the day while SPY is down about 3%, which is relative strength. It sits just under its 50-day average at 3.98, with the 200-day at 4.77.
- With ATR near 6.5% of price, a few sessions can easily move it 10% either way.

- Upside: insurance payment confirmed, revolver amendment announced, new contract or rig deployment news, further insider buys, and an oil or energy bounce.
- Downside: the insurance payment is delayed, a contracting or sanctions setback, and a broad market selloff (SPY down about 3% today).

**Read.** The insider signal and relative strength are positive. The 22% bounce already prices some of it, and the stock sits at resistance (the 50-day average, around $3.98). The binary insurance news is the key near-term driver, so check for it before sizing a position.

- **Q2 guide:** Revenue guidance is $820–830M. The non-GAAP margin guide is 27–28%.

- **Leadership uncertainty:** The undated CEO search is the clear surprise, because the numbers themselves were solid.
- **ARR:** Slowing ARR growth is the other likely cause.
- **Earlier warning:** In August the company flagged that hardware prices and delivery times were delaying customer projects and pushing contract start dates later. It said it saw no near-term letup. The Q1 results don't tell us whether that has worsened.
- **Setup:** The stock was already down 41% over 20 days and RSI is 21. That points to a heavy sell-off with some forced selling.

  - A reflex bounce from oversold levels.
  - A named CEO, which is unlikely within days.

  - The 52-week low of 34.01 is the next reference point on the downside, about 21% below the current price.

**Take:** this looks like a fundamentally decent quarter hit by a governance overhang. That makes a bounce plausible. Check today's analyst notes and the call commentary on ARR and the hardware squeeze before acting.

The argument is whether AI spending will pay off.
2. **AI financing and debt is the second thread.** Nvidia has set up a roughly $500B third-party financing program through Goldman Sachs and other firms, and it works as "the bank" for the AI ecosystem. Reports say AI debt issuance is far above last year, the Fed has flagged its rapid growth, and one lender has weighed leaving the program. The CNBC headline suggests that worry flared again on Tuesday. I couldn't find the article itself, so what it says is unconfirmed.
3. **Nvidia leadership is the least certain thread.** Earlier this month, reports said Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal, which hit AI stocks and cost Nvidia about $192B in market value. Yahoo's live blog says Nvidia rallied Friday on his reinstatement. I couldn't confirm the reinstatement independently, and one Nvidia newsroom result mentions a CEO transition with no date. - It covers regional distribution centers, e-commerce, and greenfield international sites starting with Mexico. It includes $125M of development funding.
- Revenue from it comes mainly late in fiscal 2027 and over multiple years, so it does little for near-term earnings.

- Concentration rises with this deal. One analysis puts Walmart at roughly 58-60% of the backlog, and a headline claims 87% of revenue (unverified).

- Q1 guidance was revenue of $805-825M and adjusted EBITDA of $110-120M. The revenue range was below the roughly $822M consensus.

- Operating expenses are set to rise. Gross margin is expected to be flat in the first half. Next-generation storage margin help comes in the second half of fiscal 2027.

**BN: the 13D is not an activist signal. It's a routine filing from a restructuring. The stock is down on market beta plus a post-earnings slide.**

**What the 13D is.** BN is the filer, not the target. The issuer is Brookfield Infrastructure Partners Inc. (BIP Inc.), the new single entity formed on Nov 19 when BIP and BIPC merged. BN, with BAM Partners Trust, reports 207,999,442 shares, or 26.35%. The Item 4 text says BN will "hold on a continuing basis" and "reserves the right" to influence management, which is standard boilerplate. It reports no purchases in the past 60 days and lists the plans in items (a)–(j) as none, apart from the exchange itself. The Nov 19 event was the one-for-one exchange of BIP and BIPC units into BIP Inc. shares. A matching 13D/A on BIPC (Amendment 7) was filed at the same time. BN is the controlling holder here, so nothing is being demanded of BN. I would not trade this as an event.

**The BN story.**
- **Q3 results, Nov 12.** Distributable earnings (DE) before realizations were $0.64 per share, up 14%. Total DE was $0.73, up 16%. LTM DE before realizations was $2.47 per share. Fundraising was $25B in the quarter. Buybacks were about $900M year to date.
- **Share price.** The stock still fell. The Finchannel article quoted $41.77 on Nov 12. Benzinga showed a 6.6% drop on Nov 13 and a close of $39.39 on Nov 18. Today's $38.64 is about 14.7x LTM DE before realizations.
- **Why it fell.** I found no explicit cause. The Finchannel piece names none, and I did not confirm a private-credit or wealth-solutions worry. One item I could not verify is that a Benzinga page (source of the 6.6% drop) was reached only through search snippets.
- **Analysts.** J.P. Morgan raised its target to $65 on Nov 10, with an Overweight rating. Other published targets run $51–$61. Targets are well above the price, but they are slow-moving and won't drive the next few sessions.
